Name: language_set_effort_budget
Title: How Hard Is This, in Your Language? Query Language as a Covert Effort-Budget That Mis-Allocates Reasoning Length in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: One-sentence novelty: unlike prior work on multilingual overthinking, latent English reasoning pathways, or monolingual stopping, we claim a SEPARABLE mechanism -- a shared, language-agnostic difficulty estimate versus a language-conditioned reasoning EFFORT BUDGET (a stopping/length controller) -- and show the budget is causally steerable. Concretely, multilingual LLMs carry a shared estimate of a problem's intrinsic difficulty but set how many chain-of-thought steps to spend (when to stop) via a language-conditioned scalar only loosely tied to true difficulty, so for a problem of fixed difficulty they systematically UNDERTHINK (truncate early, give up) in low-resource/typologically distant languages and can OVERTHINK in others; this mis-allocation -- distinguishable from a comprehension deficit -- contributes to the multilingual reasoning gap, and extracting an effort-budget direction and steering it re-allocates reasoning length per language and recovers accuracy without retraining.
Related Work: We position against four specific families and state one delta each. (1) Comprehension/pivoting accounts hold that low-resource reasoning fails because the model mis-understands the problem; our identification test (below) separates this from effort mis-allocation. (2) Latent-English-pathway work (Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026; Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English 2025) shows reasoning routes through an English-centered but uneven latent pathway -- it does not posit a language-set stopping controller nor steer length. (3) Monolingual stopping/overthinking controllers (When More is Less 2025, the inverted-U CoT-length result) study length as a function of difficulty and capability within one language, never as a language-conditioned budget decoupled from a shared difficulty estimate. (4) Multilingual CoT failure analyses (What Really Counts 2025; Language Mixing in Reasoning Models 2025; When Less Language is More 2025) analyze which steps/components matter or ablate language-specific components, but do not measure a per-item under/over-thinking gap attributable to language rather than difficulty, and provide no causal effort-budget direction. Our novelty is primarily a new problem framing (language sets an effort budget) plus its causal test/intervention; the mechanistic finding is secondary. Two non-obvious predictions unique to this theory that alternatives do not make: (a) FORCING more steps (or steering the budget up) in an under-thinking language recovers accuracy even though comprehension/pivoting accounts predict no gain from mere length; (b) the SAME model over-thinks (wastes steps, hurting accuracy via the inverted-U) in some languages while under-thinking in others on matched-difficulty items -- a signed, language-indexed mis-allocation a pure competence deficit cannot produce.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs reason far better in high-resource languages, a gap usually attributed to weaker reasoning ability or to comprehension failure in low-resource languages. We propose a different, testable cause: the query language covertly sets the model's reasoning EFFORT BUDGET -- how many chain-of-thought steps it spends and when it decides it is done -- and this budget is only loosely coupled to the problem's true difficulty. Under this view, for a problem of fixed difficulty the model underthinks (truncates and gives up early) in low-resource, typologically distant languages and can overthink in others, so part of the multilingual gap reflects mis-allocated effort rather than absent competence. We distinguish a shared, language-agnostic difficulty estimate from a language-conditioned effort budget that gates stopping, and give an identification criterion that separates effort mis-allocation from comprehension failure: if injecting the high-resource EFFORT signal (not the reasoning content), or forcing/steering more steps, restores correctness, the deficit is budgeting, not comprehension. Behaviorally we show that, controlling true difficulty via parallel items and multiple difficulty proxies, CoT length and early-give-up vary systematically with query language and predict accuracy loss, estimating the variance in the gap attributable to language versus comprehension. We then probe for a shared difficulty direction and use activation patching and steering -- our primary causal evidence -- to test that low-resource under-reasoning localizes to a language-set stopping controller, and to re-allocate reasoning length per language, comparing against forced-longer-CoT, English-pivot round-trip, and translate-to-English baselines. If the theory is false we still learn whether the gap is comprehension- or competence-bound, informing where to invest. The result matters for benchmark builders, multilingual model developers, inference-time-control researchers, and for accessibility/safety of low-resource deployment. Experiments span MGSM, XCOPA, and multi-hop QA across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and a distilled reasoning model.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Data: multilingual math with matched difficulty -- MGSM (existing; 250 parallel problems) plus 800 GSM-style items (scaled up for per-language/per-model power) annotated with MULTIPLE difficulty proxies (minimum required step count, human difficulty judgments, and English-reference solve rate), XCOPA commonsense (existing), and a translated 2-hop QA subset (400 items). All items are PARALLEL translations across 12 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels, with human-verified translation quality and native-speaker validation, so true difficulty is held constant across languages. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; CoT at temperature 0, 3 prompt seeds. Reasoning length is measured primarily in parsed STEPS (token counts reported separately) via a validated multilingual step-parser whose reliability is reported per language. Confound controls run throughout: comprehension-only baselines (a separate question probing whether the problem was understood), English-pivot round-trip and translate-to-English conditions, same-language paraphrase controls, and ablations for prompting format, answer language, and verbosity priors. Identification criterion (pre-registered): effort mis-allocation is supported iff, at matched difficulty and matched comprehension, (i) length varies by language and predicts errors, and (ii) supplying the effort/stopping signal or forcing more steps recovers accuracy; it is refuted if comprehension baselines fully account for the length/accuracy gap or if adding steps does not help.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- language-attributable effort mis-allocation, with a comprehension control): per item measure reasoning length in steps, EARLY-GIVE-UP rate, and accuracy, plus a comprehension score. Decisive metric: the residual reasoning-length variance attributable to LANGUAGE after regressing length on the multiple difficulty proxies AND the comprehension score (added R^2 from language beyond difficulty and comprehension), plus the correlation between under-length and wrong answers. This directly estimates how much of the gap is effort vs comprehension, so we avoid asserting 'major driver' beyond what the variance decomposition supports. Convincing result: language explains added R^2 >=0.10 beyond difficulty and comprehension, low-resource/distant languages are systematically shorter than their high-resource parallel run, and under-length predicts errors at Spearman >=0.3. Indecision band: 0.03-0.10 = weak; <0.03 = no language-attributable effort effect, refuting H2. Negative result (length explained by difficulty/comprehension) refutes the framing but still tells us the gap is comprehension-bound.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- shared difficulty estimate vs language-set budget): at each layer train (i) a difficulty probe predicting annotated step-count and (ii) a stopping probe predicting imminent final-answer emission; train in one language, test cross-lingually. Probes are treated as correlational evidence only. Decisive metric: cross-lingual transfer accuracy of the difficulty probe (contrasted with per-language variation in realized length). Convincing result: difficulty-probe cross-lingual transfer within 10 pp of in-language (shared estimate) while realized length for the same items differs by language. Indecision band: 10-25 pp below = partially shared; >25 pp below weakens H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- causal localization to a stopping controller; primary causal evidence): on parallel items solved with adequate reasoning in a high-resource language but under-reasoned/wrong in a low-resource one, (a) patch the mid-layer difficulty representation from the high-resource run into the low-resource run; (b) patch the late-layer stopping/effort signal. Cross-language patching alignment: because scripts/tokenizers differ, we align at the reasoning-step boundary positions (parsed) rather than raw token indices, patch at matched relative depth, and use identity/random-direction/wrong-layer null patches as controls to avoid script/tokenizer confounds. Decisive metric: rate at which reasoning lengthens and the answer becomes correct under each patch. Convincing result: the difficulty-patch restores correctness in <=15% of cases while the effort/stopping-patch restores adequate-length reasoning and correctness in >=40%, beating null controls -- localizing the gap to a language-set stopping controller. Indecision band: effort-patch 20-40% = partial; <20%, controls match, or difficulty-patch > effort-patch = refutes localization, favoring a competence/comprehension deficit.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- effort-budget steering recovers accuracy without retraining; quantified upside): extract an effort-budget direction (mean activation difference between long- and short-reasoning continue-vs-stop states pooled across languages); steer to LENGTHEN in under-thinking languages and SHORTEN in over-thinking ones. Systems compared: steering vs forced-longer-CoT prompting vs best-of-length voting vs English-pivot round-trip vs translate-to-English-first vs matched-norm random-direction steering (sham). Decisive metrics (in order): accuracy gain on under-thinking languages and the fraction of the translate-to-English gap it closes (quantifying upside relative to the translate-to-English ceiling and at zero retraining cost); change in CoT length and give-up rate; output-language fidelity; fluency (perplexity); specificity that shortening over-thinking items preserves accuracy. Convincing result: steering raises under-thinking-language accuracy by >=4 points over no intervention, closes a substantial fraction of the translate-to-English gap, matches or beats forced-longer-CoT, beats the sham control, without harming output-language fidelity (>=95% correct language) or inflating length on already-adequate items. Indecision band: 1.5-4 points = partial; <1.5, or gains only via uncontrolled rambling that hurts other items, or sham matches it = refutes the steerable-budget claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Reasoning length is confounded with tokenizer efficiency across scripts; we measure length in parsed STEPS as the primary unit, report token counts separately, and hold true difficulty fixed via parallel items. 2. Probe decodability of a 'difficulty' or 'effort' signal is correlational and may reflect the readout basis; the causal patching (Exp. 3) and steering (Exp. 4), with null/sham controls, are the primary causal evidence, and we temper causal language for probe results. 3. Under-reasoning could genuinely reflect weaker competence OR comprehension failure, not mis-allocated effort; the comprehension-only baselines, the variance decomposition (Exp. 1), and the pre-registered identification criterion (does injecting the effort signal / forcing steps recover accuracy?) distinguish these, and we avoid claiming 'major driver' beyond the estimated variance explained. 4. Steering to lengthen may induce rambling/overthinking that hurts accuracy (inverted-U); we tune dose and report the full length-accuracy trade-off and specificity controls. 5. Parsing steps and detecting give-up across languages is noisy; we use a validated multilingual step-parser with reliability reported per language, human spot-checks, and native-speaker validation of translations. 6. Prompt format, answer language, and verbosity priors could drive apparent length differences; these are explicit ablations. 7. Strong models may allocate effort well, shrinking the effect; low-resource languages, harder items, the reasoning-distilled model, and the scaled-up 800-item set provide power. 8. If the theory is false, the design still identifies whether the gap is comprehension- or competence-bound, an informative outcome. 9. Findings may be model-specific; four models across families address but do not exhaust generality.
